No. 001 · Fantasy Football · August 2026
The Numbers Behind the Noise

The Buzz
Is Real

Is Travis Hunter wearing teal? Is the Santa Clara electrical substation haunted? Are the Vikings seriously considering going with J.J. McCarthy over Kyler Murray? It's camp season, baby. Every year we get storylines. In this report we backtested the camp buzz over eight years, and we're tracking everything going on through the month of August.

By Nick Gurol · Data through August 2, 2026
Companion board Training Camp Dashboard — all 32 clubs →
The Front Page · three live trackers
JAXThe Teal Tracker

Is Travis Hunter a receiver or a corner this year?

Nine months after the knee injury that ended his rookie year ten games early, Hunter is a full participant, ten pounds heavier, clocked at 22.6 mph. The tell from last summer: he leaned into one side of the ball early in camp before going two-way. So the tracker watches for the lean.

WR ↔ CB Lean MeterUpdated Aug 2
WR
CB
  • AUG 2Two catches, one over his shoulder down the sideline and one on a deep over, plus an INT. "Maybe most impressive practice of his career." Snap tracker through four days: 34 defense, 22 offense (Michael DiRocco, ESPN). Judy Battista of NFL Network saw the same thing: "deep catches, interceptions."
  • AUG 2"Travis Hunter day!" per Frank Frangie, the team's radio voice, from the sideline: "If you were here, you saw it. If not, you'll read plenty about it on social. But, wow." Which side of the ball made the wow? Tonight's reports will say.
  • JUL 31Day 3: both sides again. "I definitely do feel free. They let me go out there and just do my thing."
  • JUL 30Day 2: offense and defense, full participant. Coen still planning managed reps.
  • JUL 29Day 1: practices both ways in his return from the knee. "Doesn't feel like I'm coming off an injury."
Current lean: corner, 34 defensive snaps to 22 offensive through four days, per DiRocco's tracker. The lean the tracker was built to catch is here, just pointing the other way from last summer.

SFThe Substation Grim Reaper

Something keeps claiming 49ers players, and George Kittle blames the power grid

Kittle blames electromagnetic fields coming off the substation beside the Santa Clara facility, where the 49ers have been the league's most-injured team since 2014. The NFL's medical office waved it off. The reaper did not.

Reaper BoardUpdated Aug 2
1
Days since the substation
claimed a 49er
  • AUG 1Brock Purdy: severe concussion. The reaper goes quarterback hunting.
  • DAY 1Christian Kirk: calf strain, one practice into his 49ers tenure.
  • DAY 1Vederian Lowe: high ankle sprain, extended absence.
  • DAY 1Gracen Halton: knee bone bruise · Andrew Farmer: back.
  • PRIORGeorge Kittle: Achilles, playoffs. The theorist is also a victim.
Camp toll: 5 players · Fantasy fallout: Stribling's path (watchlist), Mac Jones stock, Kittle discount.
The conspiracy · NFL response · 49ers will look into it
MINThe QB Duel

Kyler Murray vs. J.J. McCarthy, and the tape disagrees with the talent

Murray has the pedigree; McCarthy has the completions and, per beat reporting, the locker room. Murray is learning a new offense off a foot injury, which is exactly the "established name catching negative August coverage" pattern that busted 79% of the time in the backtest.

Duel ScoreboardUpdated Aug 2

  • AUG 1Murray "wins the day" at the fan-open practice. Battle officially live.
  • JUL 31Charted periods through two days favor McCarthy across the board.
  • JUL 30Beat reporting: "early vibes" say the locker room leans McCarthy.
Current lean: McCarthy, with Murray's talent keeping the door open.

TLDR · five players to watch

The backtest below says the names worth chasing are the ones nobody had penciled in as starters who are getting written about right now. Five out of the 2026 wire:

  • Jonathon Brooks CAR RB
    “He looks like the guy that I remember” · first-team reps with Chuba Hubbard underperforming.
  • Malik Washington MIA WR
    “do-it-all weapon” · being prioritized in Miami’s offense.
  • Zachariah Branch ATL WR
    “nightmare for opposing cornerbacks” · deep-threat role forming.
  • Matthew Golden GB WR
    “off to a strong start in camp” · year-2 receiver stacking good practices.
  • Quinshon Judkins CLE RB
    “all three downs” · that’s his RB coach, Duce Staley, describing the role.

The full list is in the watchlist, and we keep adding to it as reports come in through August.

The whole thing started with a text. My buddy Glen, 2:29 on a Saturday afternoon.

Today 2:29 PM
Glen
Nick you know what a fun little Claude side quest I would enjoy is?
How predictive are reports from training camp? Like keyword searching "popping" or "tough day" for guys that aren't projected as starters prior to training camp

It's a great question because everyone in your league already trades on this signal without knowing its value. Somebody drafted Puka Nacua in August 2023 because a beat writer wrote "glowing reviews since the beginning of OTAs." Somebody else ignored it. One of them won the league. The question is which one was playing the odds right.

Let's put the camp buzz to the test.

If you read nothing else

This study is about the players nobody had penciled in before camp: backups, late-round rookies, journeymen, post-hype guys. Not established starters, and not first-round rookies. The ones in that group who generate positive training camp buzz finish as fantasy starters about 16% of the time. The ones nobody writes about? 1.3%. That's a 13x jump, it showed up in all eight seasons we tested, and it survives every control we threw at it. It still misses five times out of six. And 13 guys fit the profile right now, one week into 2026 camp.

The Camp WireLive · 2026
Every buzz mention in the study, newest first. The 2026 feed now folds in beat-reporter tweets, harvested from liveblogs and roundups that embed them, with the reporter credited on each item. Tap a year to open it, tap a headline to read the source. Inside each year, "Team by team" collects each club's buzz with how the season actually ended. One note on method: these items aggregate headlines and the short quote that came with them, so whatever nuance the reporter put in the body of the article is probably missed here. This is a read on overall sentiment, not a deep read of any one story.

The 2018–2025 wires — every mention in the study, with how each season actually ended — now live at the bottom of the page. Jump to the archive ↓

01 What we actually did

We collected 95 camp-window articles from 2018 through 2025, the stuff written in late July and August while practice was actually happening: NFL.com camp reports, CBS and SI stock watches, PFF risers, FantasyPros trackers, WalterFootball's camp diaries. The live 2026 pipeline also reads Establish The Run, Underdog Fantasy, and beat-writer tweets via X. From those articles we pulled 690 player mentions, each tagged with the exact language ("turning heads," "standing out," "popping," "tough day," "falling behind") and a sentiment direction.

Then we matched every mention to real season outcomes, and to the full population of players who did not get any buzz. The question we are trying to answer is whether camp buzz helps predict in-season success, and you can only answer that against the players nobody wrote about.

How the study works
Tap "more detail" on any step
1
Collect the coverage 95 articles
Camp-window reporting from 2018–2025, plus live 2026.
More detail
Sources: NFL.com, CBS Sports, SI, PFF, FantasyPros, Fantasy Points, Bleacher Report, WalterFootball, Yahoo, and team beat outlets. The live 2026 feed adds Establish The Run, Underdog Fantasy, and beat-writer tweets via X. Only articles published mid-July through early September of each season, so the coverage reflects what was knowable at the time.
2
Tag every player mention 690 mentions
Sentiment plus the exact quote. “Practices like a pro” is data.
More detail
Each mention keeps the verbatim phrase, the direction (positive or negative), the source URL, and any depth-chart context the writer gave. A player mentioned in three articles gets three rows, later aggregated by majority direction.
3
Match to real players 99% match rate
Every mention linked to an nflverse player ID.
More detail
Names normalized (suffixes stripped, punctuation removed) and joined to nflverse player IDs by name, position, and season roster. 638 of 645 offensive-position mentions matched. The 7 misses were practice-squad names that never made a roster file.
4
Classify the depth chart 7,835 player-seasons
Every rostered QB, RB, WR, TE labeled pre-camp: projected starter or not. About 800 non-starters per season.
More detail
A player counts as a projected starter entering camp if any of these held: round-1 rookie draft capital, a startable positional finish the prior season, startable points-per-game in an injury-shortened prior season, or a 60%+ average offensive snap share across 8+ games the prior season. Everything in this rule uses information available BEFORE camp opened. Nothing from the season being predicted leaks in.
5
Score the seasons binary outcome
Did the player finish startable at his position?
More detail
Outcome: total PPR points from nflverse weekly stats, converted to a positional finish rank. “Startable” = top-12 QB, top-24 RB, top-36 WR, top-12 TE. A stricter “top tier” outcome (QB6/RB12/WR18/TE6) was tested too and shows the same lift.
6
Compare against silence buzz vs 6,094 quiet players
Hit rates, the size of the gap, and the controls that try to kill the result.
More detail
Buzz group vs no-buzz group, 2x2 tables, Fisher exact tests. Then the same comparison repeated inside subgroups: by position, by season, by rookie draft round, by prior production. If the effect were an artifact of one of those variables, it would vanish inside the subgroups. It doesn't.
Every number above is reproducible from the data files.

02 The headline number

Take the non-projected starters. The backups, the day-3 rookies, the journeymen, the post-hype guys. About 6,400 of them across eight seasons. Then split them by August coverage.

Sixteen percent doesn't sound like much until you price the alternative. A quiet deep-roster guy hits about once in 77 tries. A buzzy one hits once in six. In a 12-team league, the difference between those two odds, applied to your last three bench spots, is roughly the difference between streaming waivers all year and rostering Sam LaPorta in the 14th round.

The strangest thing the study turned up is that most of the signal is just attention. Whether the coverage was good or bad mattered far less than whether anybody wrote about the player at all.

Players catching negative camp coverage hit at 13.4% when they weren't projected starters, ten times the rate of players with no coverage at all. The mechanism is mundane: writers cover live position battles, so a backup taking "tough day" criticism is a backup standing close enough to a job to be criticized. Marlon Mack, Rachaad White, and Travis Etienne in 2025 all delivered startable seasons in years when camp reporters were doubting them. A limitation to flag here: the cohort is built by a rules-based filter, and a few names it treats as non-starters would have looked like starters to any human in August. The strict cohort in the next section ejects those cases. One more caution before you read "no coverage" as doom: in this study that label means absent from the 95 articles we collected, not absent from every beat report in America. The limitations section takes that seriously.

03 Eight for eight

A 13x lift built on one magical season would be a trivia answer, not a strategy. So here is the year-by-year. The chart uses the strict cohort, which is the harder test of the two we ran. On top of dropping everyone we could call a projected starter from pre-camp information, it also drops veterans who finished startable in any of the three previous seasons. That controls for the comeback story: a spreadsheet thinks a guy who missed all of last year is a nobody, and you don't. The full cohort, with those veterans left in, is one tap below the chart.

Buzz beats silence in every season under both definitions. The size of the gap swings a lot, from single digits in the leanest years to the mid-thirties in 2023's LaPorta-Nacua-Kyren bonanza, so it is a rate you play across a lot of picks rather than a read on any one guy.

The year-by-year receipts behind this chart, every mention from 2018 to 2025, are in the archive at the bottom of the page.

04 Isn't this just high drafted rookies winning a starting job?

That was our first objection too. It's why round-1 rookies were excluded from the cohort up front, and it's why the next chart exists. Split the cohort by pedigree and run the comparison inside each group.

Draft capital definitely matters. But when we control for it, the rookies who get talked about outperform the ones who don't. And, interestingly, veterans who were not startable the year before and then pick up buzz also outperform the veterans without it, even after we control for the guys coming back from injury. That's probably all we have to say here.

The one dead zone: undrafted free agents. UDFA camp heroes went 0-for-8. Jake Kumerow, "practices like a pro," source: Aaron Rodgers, is the patron saint of that group, and the reason "coach loves an UDFA" should move your heart and not your queue.

Bonus finding for the pessimists. Flip the whole study around and look at projected starters catching negative August coverage. They busted 79% of the time, against 61% for starters with quiet camps, a gap far too consistent across 1,200 starter-seasons to be noise. The “tough day” keyword works. It just works on the guys you drafted in round four, not the ones you're stashing in round fourteen.

05 The watchlist, right now

Here's the part you can use tonight. Same filter, applied live: non-projected starters generating positive buzz one week into 2026 camp, coverage through August 1. History's rate card says about three of these eighteen finish startable. History also says one week of practice reports is the noisy early read, and it's already claimed a victim: Chris Brazzell II popped in Carolina's first week, then tore his LCL. This list wants a late-August refresh before you draft on it, and we keep adding to it as more reports come in. We have a lot more sources feeding the pipeline now, so expect it to grow, and to get sorted by how strong the buzz is as the sample fills out.

06 Into the weeds

For anyone who wants a deeper dive into the data science behind this, here is the full breakdown, limitations included. One thing worth saying out loud: this study was made possible by the sentiment analysis you get out of Claude. The new LLM tooling makes it much easier to take a big pile of text and run a real historical study on it. Refining that process is going to be worth a lot, and it is the kind of work I want to do more of on The Side Quest.

The model, precisely

Unit of analysis: the player-season. The exposure variable is categorical with three levels, built by aggregating all of a player's tagged mentions in one camp window by majority direction: positive, negative, or none (mixed ties, 26 cases, analyzed separately and excluded from the headline numbers). The outcome is binary: startable positional finish by total PPR points, thresholds QB12 / RB24 / WR36 / TE12, computed from nflverse weekly data.

In plain terms: sentiment-labeled camp coverage is a categorical predictor of a binary fantasy outcome, measured on a cohort of non-projected starters that is defined only from pre-camp information. We chose stratified contingency tables over logistic regression on purpose. With 44 total hits in the buzz group, piling several covariates into a regression would mostly be overfitting, and stratification shows you exactly where the effect lives instead of averaging over it. We also checked a continuous version of the outcome: median PPR points per game among players who saw the field is 7.3 for the buzz group vs 3.6 for the quiet group.

The projected-starter rule is simple. A player counts as a projected starter if any one of these four things was true before camp opened: round-1 rookie draft capital; a startable finish the prior season (6-game minimum); startable points per game the prior season (5-game minimum, which catches stars who missed half a year); or a 60%+ average offensive snap share across 8+ games the prior season (which catches low-scoring every-down players). Anyone who fails all four is in the cohort.

On a holdout: there isn't a separate one. Every season is used to compute the headline numbers. What stands in for a holdout is running the same comparison inside each of the eight camp windows on its own, which is the season-by-season check in the next panel, and buzz wins all eight.

Here is how the sentiment labels themselves are distributed across the eight camp windows.

Validation: how we tried to kill it

Test one, significance: a 2x2 Fisher exact test on buzz vs none, p = 1.7 × 10⁻³⁰. With effect sizes this large the p-value is almost beside the point; the question is bias, not chance.

Test two, temporal stability: the comparison re-run within each of the eight seasons independently, which is season-level cross-validation in everything but name. Buzz wins all eight. A single-era artifact (rule changes, coverage volume changes, one crazy rookie class) would show holes here.

Test three, positional stability: re-run within each position. QB +19.6 points of hit rate, RB +15.7, WR +12.9, TE +20.6, all significant. No single position carries it.

Test four, the leakage audit: the classifier flagged 19 buzz players as "non-projected starters" who had startable seasons within the previous three years, the returning-from-injury crowd, which is the kind of leakage that can manufacture a result. Ejecting all of them (the strict cohort, the one charted above) widens the gap instead of closing it.

Test five, outcome sensitivity: swap the startable threshold for a harsher top-tier one (QB6/RB12/WR18/TE6). Lift holds at 12x (5.2% vs 0.43%).

What this can't tell you

The "no buzz" label only means a player was absent from the 95 articles we collected, not that nobody wrote about him. The corpus leans national, and it misses local beat coverage entirely. You can see the leak in the control group's own hit list: James Conner and Phillip Lindsay in 2018, James Robinson in 2020, and George Kittle in 2018 all count as "quiet" here despite having had real August coverage in outlets we didn't capture. Note which way this cuts, though. False quiets inflate the 1.3% base rate, so the true buzz-vs-silence gap is wider than 13x, not narrower. What the leak does break is any strong claim about silence itself: "not in our corpus" is weaker evidence than "nobody talked about him." More articles would simply be better, and I am fixing that by hand, adding more and more feeds to the automated headline-grabbing pipeline I built. We can backtest 2026 specifically next year.

The outcome here is "became fantasy-relevant," not "beat his draft price." Historical intra-August ADP wasn't retrievable for this build, and late-August ADP already chases this exact signal. The full 13x edge exists only against opponents who ignore camp news entirely; against a sharp room, the residual edge is whatever the market underweights, which the sample suggests is not zero (LaPorta and Nacua were still nearly free on draft day) but is not 13x either. Uncertainty follows a lot of these players, and you usually get a discount in ADP for it, so I am fine with this limitation.

Buzz is media-curated, not raw practice performance. Writers mention players who already have opportunity: an injury ahead of them, an open depth chart. The signal you're buying is a bundle of performance and situation. That's fine, because it's the same bundle you consume as a reader, but don't mistake this for "practice reps predict production" in isolation.

Then there is article survivorship. We could only collect coverage that stayed indexed for up to eight years, which tilts toward major outlets. If big-outlet buzz is systematically better than small-outlet buzz, our estimate is too high for the buzz you'd scrape from everything; if attention from anywhere is what matters (and the negative-buzz finding hints it is), the bias is small. The direction of the result survives every one of these caveats.
